tool.name: pathlib
tool.tagline: Object-oriented file system paths that work the same on every OS
tool.description: pathlib represents file system paths as objects with methods for joining, inspecting, reading, writing, globbing and resolving them. It replaces most uses of os.path, glob and open with one readable API that handles Windows and POSIX differences. It's the modern default for any Python code that touches files.

concepts.name: Path objects and the / operator
concepts.summary: Create Path objects, join them with /, and get the current and home directories.
concepts.why: Path objects make file code shorter, more readable and portable compared with string juggling.
concepts.body:
`from pathlib import Path` gives you the class you'll use almost all the time. `Path("data/input.csv")` creates a path object; on Windows it becomes a `WindowsPath`, elsewhere a `PosixPath`, but you rarely need to care.

Join paths with the **/ operator**:

```python
base = Path("data")
report = base / "2024" / "report.csv"
```

Strings can appear on either side (`"logs" / Path("x")` works too), and the right separator is used for the platform. As with `os.path.join`, joining an absolute path discards what came before: `Path("data") / "/etc"` is `/etc`.

Useful starting points:

- `Path.cwd()` the current working directory
- `Path.home()` the user's home directory
- `Path(__file__).parent` the folder containing the current module, the reliable base for files shipped with your code

`str(p)` converts back to a string when an API really needs one, but nearly all of the standard library (`open`, `os`, `shutil`, `subprocess`, `json`...) accepts Path objects directly, because Path implements the `os.PathLike` protocol.

Paths are **immutable** and hashable: methods return new paths, and you can use them as dict keys or in sets. Comparing paths compares their parts, case-insensitively on Windows.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

base = Path("data")
report = base / "2024" / "report.csv"
print(report)                    # data/2024/report.csv
print(type(report).__name__)     # PosixPath
print(Path("data") / "/etc")     # /etc

print(Path.home().is_absolute())  # True
print(Path.cwd() == Path(".").resolve())  # True

seen = {Path("a/b"), Path("a") / "b"}
print(len(seen))                 # 1
here = Path(__file__).parent if "__file__" in globals() else Path.cwd()
print(here.is_dir())             # True
takeaways: `Path(...) / 'name'` joins paths portably
`Path.cwd()`, `Path.home()` and `Path(__file__).parent` are common bases
Paths are immutable, hashable and accepted by open, os and shutil
pitfalls: Concatenating strings with '/' and passing them around instead of keeping Path objects.

quiz.explain: The / operator joins segments with the platform separator and returns a new relative Path.

concepts.name: Names, suffixes and parents
concepts.summary: Take paths apart with name, stem, suffix, parent and parts, and derive new paths with with_name, with_stem and with_suffix.
concepts.why: Renaming outputs, grouping files by extension and finding sibling files are everyday tasks.
concepts.body:
A path exposes its components as properties, all computed from the string without touching the disk:

- `p.name` final component: `report.tar.gz`
- `p.suffix` last extension: `.gz`; `p.suffixes`: `['.tar', '.gz']`
- `p.stem` name without the last suffix: `report.tar`
- `p.parent` the containing path; `p.parents` all ancestors, indexable (`p.parents[1]`)
- `p.parts` a tuple of components; `p.anchor` the drive and root (`/` or `C:\`)

To derive related paths, use the `with_*` methods, which return new paths:

- `p.with_suffix(".json")` replaces the last suffix (pass `""` to remove it)
- `p.with_name("other.txt")` replaces the final component
- `p.with_stem("report-v2")` keeps the suffix and changes the stem

Typical pattern: write `out = src.with_suffix(".processed.csv")` or put outputs next to inputs with `src.parent / f"{src.stem}.out"`.

Gotchas: `suffix` only sees the last dot, so `.tar.gz` needs `suffixes`; a leading dot file like `.bashrc` has no suffix (its stem is `.bashrc`). The parent of a relative single name is `Path(".")`, and the parent of `/` is `/` itself.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("/srv/backups/db.2025-03-01.tar.gz")
print(p.name)            # db.2025-03-01.tar.gz
print(p.stem)            # db.2025-03-01.tar
print(p.suffix)          # .gz
print(p.suffixes)        # ['.2025-03-01', '.tar', '.gz']
print(p.parent)          # /srv/backups
print(p.parents[1])      # /srv
print(p.parts[:3])       # ('/', 'srv', 'backups')

src = Path("photos/cat.jpeg")
print(src.with_suffix(".png"))     # photos/cat.png
print(src.with_stem("cat_small"))  # photos/cat_small.jpeg
print(Path(".bashrc").suffix == "")  # True
print(Path("notes.txt").parent)    # .
takeaways: `name`, `stem`, `suffix`, `parent` and `parts` are pure string operations
`with_suffix`, `with_name` and `with_stem` derive new paths
Dots in names are tricky: use `suffixes` for multi-part extensions
pitfalls: Expecting `suffix` to return '.tar.gz'; it only returns the last extension.

quiz.explain: with_suffix replaces only the last suffix, '.gz'.

concepts.name: Reading and writing files
concepts.summary: Read and write whole files with read_text, write_text, read_bytes and write_bytes, or open a Path for streaming.
concepts.why: Small files can be read or written in one call, without boilerplate.
concepts.body:
For small and medium files, Path has one-call helpers:

- `p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` returns the whole file as a str.
- `p.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")` creates or **overwrites** the file and returns the number of characters written.
- `p.read_bytes()` and `p.write_bytes(data)` do the same for binary data.

Each call opens and closes the file for you. Always pass `encoding=` for text: the default is the locale encoding, which differs between machines (Python 3.15 will switch to UTF-8 by default). `read_text` in 3.13 also accepts `newline=`.

For large files, or to process line by line, use `p.open()`, which takes the same arguments as the built-in `open`:

```python
with p.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        ...
```

`write_text` doesn't create missing parent directories; call `p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` first. To append, use `p.open("a")`; there is no `append_text`.

`read_text` loads everything into memory and decodes it at once. That's ideal for config files and templates, but avoid it for multi-gigabyte logs.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

out = Path("build") / "hello.txt"
out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print(out.write_text("héllo\nworld\n", encoding="utf-8"))  # 12
print(out.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines())  # ['héllo', 'world']
print(len(out.read_bytes()))      # 13  (é is 2 bytes in UTF-8)

with out.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:   # append
    f.write("again\n")

with out.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(sum(1 for _ in f))      # 3
takeaways: `read_text`/`write_text` handle open and close in one call
Always pass `encoding="utf-8"` for text files
Use `p.open()` for large files, streaming or appending
pitfalls: Calling `write_text` on a path whose folder doesn't exist yet; it raises FileNotFoundError.

quiz.q: What does Path('log.txt').write_text('new') do if log.txt already has content?
quiz.explain: write_text opens the file in 'w' mode, which truncates it first.

concepts.name: Checking and listing paths
concepts.summary: Test whether paths exist and what they are, and list a directory's children with iterdir.
concepts.why: Scripts constantly need to know whether an input exists and what files a folder holds.
concepts.body:
These methods ask the file system:

- `p.exists()` true if anything is there (following symlinks)
- `p.is_file()`, `p.is_dir()`, `p.is_symlink()`
- `p.stat().st_size` size in bytes, `p.stat().st_mtime` modification time

They return `False` rather than raising when the path is missing or inaccessible. Since 3.12, `exists`, `is_file` and `is_dir` take `follow_symlinks=False` to inspect links themselves.

`p.iterdir()` yields a Path for each entry in the directory, already joined with `p`, in arbitrary order. Unlike `os.listdir`, you get usable paths, not bare names:

```python
csvs = sorted(f for f in folder.iterdir() if f.suffix == ".csv")
```

`iterdir` raises `NotADirectoryError` if `p` is a file and `FileNotFoundError` if it's missing.

Checking before acting is fine for user-facing messages ("input file not found"), but for correctness it can race: the file can vanish between `exists()` and `read_text()`. When it matters, just attempt the operation and catch `FileNotFoundError`.

For recursive listings, use `glob`/`rglob` or `Path.walk()` instead of nesting `iterdir` calls by hand.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("inbox")
folder.mkdir()
for name in ["b.csv", "a.csv", "readme.md"]:
    (folder / name).write_text("x", encoding="utf-8")
(folder / "archive").mkdir()

print(folder.exists(), folder.is_dir())          # True True
print(sorted(p.name for p in folder.iterdir()))  # ['a.csv', 'archive', 'b.csv', 'readme.md']
csvs = sorted(p for p in folder.iterdir() if p.is_file() and p.suffix == ".csv")
print(csvs)          # [PosixPath('inbox/a.csv'), PosixPath('inbox/b.csv')]
print((folder / "nope.txt").exists())            # False
print((folder / "a.csv").stat().st_size)         # 1
takeaways: `exists`, `is_file` and `is_dir` return False instead of raising
`iterdir()` yields full Path objects in arbitrary order
Prefer try/except over check-then-act when correctness matters
pitfalls: Sorting by assuming iterdir returns alphabetical order; it doesn't.

quiz.q: folder = Path('docs'). What does next(folder.iterdir()) return if docs contains intro.md?
quiz.explain: iterdir yields paths joined with the directory, ready to open.

concepts.name: Globbing with glob and rglob
concepts.summary: Find files by pattern with glob and recursively with rglob or **.
concepts.why: Collecting inputs like 'every .py file in the project' is a one-liner with glob.
concepts.body:
`p.glob(pattern)` yields paths below `p` that match a shell-style pattern:

- `*` matches any characters within one path component
- `?` matches one character; `[abc]` a character set
- `**` matches any number of directories, including none

So `p.glob("*.csv")` searches one level, `p.glob("**/*.csv")` the whole tree, and `p.rglob("*.csv")` is shorthand for the latter. Results come in arbitrary order; sort them for stable output.

Details worth knowing:

- Hidden files (starting with `.`) are matched by `*`, unlike in most shells.
- Matching follows the platform's case rules by default; pass `case_sensitive=True/False` (3.12+) to override.
- In 3.13, a pattern ending in `**` yields both files and directories; earlier versions yielded only directories. Add `/*` or a suffix pattern if you want files only.
- `glob` returns a generator; wrap in `list()` or `sorted()` to reuse the results.
- Symlinked directories are not followed by `**` unless you pass `recurse_symlinks=True` (3.13).

To exclude directories such as `.git` or `node_modules`, filter the results (`".git" not in p.parts`), or use `Path.walk()` where you can prune whole subtrees for speed.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

for f in ["src/app.py", "src/util/io.py", "src/util/README.md",
          "tests/test_app.py", ".venv/lib/x.py"]:
    p = Path(f)
    p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    p.touch()

root = Path(".")
print(sorted(map(str, root.glob("src/*.py"))))   # ['src/app.py']
py = sorted(str(p) for p in root.rglob("*.py") if ".venv" not in p.parts)
print(py)    # ['src/app.py', 'src/util/io.py', 'tests/test_app.py']
print(sorted(p.name for p in root.glob("**/test_*.py")))  # ['test_app.py']
print(len(list(root.glob("src/util/*.MD", case_sensitive=False))))  # 1
takeaways: `glob('*.ext')` searches one level; `rglob('*.ext')` or `glob('**/*.ext')` the whole tree
Results are unordered generators; sort and list them as needed
Filter by `p.parts` or use `Path.walk` to skip folders like .venv
pitfalls: Expecting `glob('*.py')` to search subdirectories; it only looks one level deep.

quiz.q: Which call finds config.yaml files in a folder and all its subfolders?
quiz.explain: rglob prefixes the pattern with **/, searching recursively.

concepts.name: Creating, moving and deleting
concepts.summary: Make directories, touch, rename, replace and delete files and empty folders with Path methods.
concepts.why: Output folders, temp files and archiving steps are part of nearly every script.
concepts.body:
Path wraps the common file operations:

- `p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` creates the directory and missing parents, and doesn't complain if it exists.
- `p.touch()` creates an empty file or updates its modification time; `touch(exist_ok=False)` fails if it exists.
- `p.rename(target)` moves or renames and returns the new Path. On Windows it fails if `target` exists.
- `p.replace(target)` does the same but overwrites `target` on every platform (atomic on POSIX).
- `p.unlink(missing_ok=True)` deletes a file, ignoring it if absent.
- `p.rmdir()` deletes an **empty** directory.

Relative targets in `rename` and `replace` are interpreted relative to the current working directory, not to `p`'s folder. Write `p.rename(p.with_name("new.txt"))` or `p.parent / "new.txt"` to stay in the same directory.

Pathlib in 3.13 has no recursive delete or copy; use `shutil.rmtree(p)`, `shutil.copy2(src, dst)` and `shutil.move(src, dst)`, which all accept Path objects. (Python 3.14 adds `Path.copy` and `Path.move`.)

All these methods raise the usual `OSError` subclasses: `FileExistsError`, `FileNotFoundError`, `IsADirectoryError`, `PermissionError`.
concepts.code:
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

out = Path("out/2025/03")
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
draft = out / "draft.txt"
draft.write_text("v1", encoding="utf-8")

final = draft.rename(draft.with_name("final.txt"))   # same folder
print(final)                          # out/2025/03/final.txt
print(draft.exists())                 # False

(out / "tmp.lock").touch()
(out / "tmp.lock").unlink()
(out / "tmp.lock").unlink(missing_ok=True)   # no error when absent

try:
    Path("out").rmdir()
except OSError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)           # OSError
shutil.rmtree("out")
print(Path("out").exists())           # False
takeaways: `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` ensures a folder exists
`rename` targets are relative to the cwd; build them from `p.parent` or `with_name`
Use shutil for recursive delete, copy and cross-device moves
pitfalls: Writing `p.rename('new.txt')` and finding the file moved into the current working directory.

quiz.q: p = Path('data/raw/a.csv'). Where does p.rename('b.csv') put the file?
options: b.csv in the current working directory
quiz.explain: A relative target is resolved against the cwd, not the file's own directory.

concepts.name: Absolute, resolved and relative paths
concepts.summary: Normalise paths with resolve and absolute, expand ~, and compute paths relative to a base with relative_to.
concepts.why: Comparing paths, printing friendly names and checking containment all need normalised paths.
concepts.body:
Three ways to make a path absolute:

- `p.absolute()` prefixes the cwd; it doesn't touch `..` or symlinks.
- `p.resolve()` makes it absolute **and** removes `..` and symlinks, giving the canonical location. Use it before comparing paths or checking containment. With `strict=True` it raises if the path doesn't exist.
- `p.expanduser()` replaces a leading `~` with the home directory. Paths never expand `~` automatically.

`p.relative_to(base)` returns the part of `p` below `base`: `Path("/srv/app/static/a.css").relative_to("/srv/app")` gives `static/a.css`. It raises `ValueError` if `p` isn't under `base`. Since 3.12, `walk_up=True` allows results with `..` segments.

`p.is_relative_to(base)` returns a bool instead of raising, but it compares **strings of parts**, not real locations: `Path("/srv/app/../etc")` "is relative to" `/srv/app`. Resolve both sides first when the path comes from users.

`p.samefile(other)` checks whether two paths point to the same file on disk, accounting for links.

Pure string normalisation like `os.path.normpath` has no direct pathlib equivalent, because collapsing `a/link/..` without asking the file system can be wrong when `link` is a symlink.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

Path("site/static").mkdir(parents=True)
Path("site/static/a.css").touch()
Path("site/latest").symlink_to("static")

p = Path("site/static/../static/a.css")
print(p.absolute() == Path.cwd() / p)          # True: no normalisation
print(p.resolve() == Path.cwd() / "site/static/a.css")   # True
print(Path("site/latest/a.css").resolve().parent.name)   # static

print(Path("/srv/app/static/a.css").relative_to("/srv/app"))  # static/a.css
print(Path("/srv/app").relative_to("/srv/app/static", walk_up=True))  # ..
print(Path("/srv/app/../etc").is_relative_to("/srv/app"))   # True (!)
print(Path("~/notes").expanduser().is_absolute())           # True
takeaways: `resolve()` canonicalises: absolute, no `..`, symlinks followed
`relative_to` strips a base prefix and raises if the path isn't under it
`is_relative_to` is lexical; resolve user-supplied paths first
pitfalls: Treating `Path('~/x')` as the home folder without calling `expanduser()`.

quiz.q: Which call gives a canonical path suitable for checking whether two paths refer to the same location?
quiz.explain: resolve makes the path absolute and eliminates .. segments and symlinks.

concepts.name: Walking trees and file metadata
concepts.summary: Traverse directory trees with Path.walk, prune subtrees, and use stat results for size and age based processing.
concepts.why: Cleanup jobs, disk-usage reports and incremental builds need to visit every file with its metadata.
concepts.body:
`Path.walk()` (3.12+) is pathlib's version of `os.walk`. It yields `(dirpath, dirnames, filenames)` for each directory, with `dirpath` as a Path and the other two as lists of names:

```python
for root, dirs, files in Path("proj").walk():
    dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if d not in {".git", "node_modules"}]
```

Editing `dirs` in place prunes the walk, which is much faster than filtering `rglob` results after the fact because pruned directories are never listed. Use `top_down=False` to visit children first (needed for deleting directories), and `on_error=` to handle unreadable folders; by default errors are ignored.

Each file's metadata comes from `path.stat()`:

- `st_size` in bytes
- `st_mtime` modification time as a POSIX timestamp; compare with `time.time()` or convert with `datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, tz=timezone.utc)`

A typical maintenance job, "delete logs older than 30 days", combines `walk` or `glob`, `stat().st_mtime` and `unlink`.

`p.stat()` follows symlinks; `p.lstat()` (or `stat(follow_symlinks=False)`) describes the link. `p.owner()` and `p.group()` give names on Unix, and `p.chmod(0o644)` changes permissions.
concepts.code:
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

for f in ["logs/app.log", "logs/old/2023.log", ".git/HEAD"]:
    Path(f).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    Path(f).write_text("x" * 100, encoding="utf-8")
month_ago = time.time() - 31 * 86400
os.utime("logs/old/2023.log", (month_ago, month_ago))

sizes, stale = {}, []
for root, dirs, files in Path(".").walk():
    dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if not d.startswith(".")]     # prune .git
    for name in files:
        st = (root / name).stat()
        sizes[str(root / name)] = st.st_size
        if st.st_mtime < time.time() - 30 * 86400:
            stale.append(root / name)
print(sorted(sizes))      # ['logs/app.log', 'logs/old/2023.log']
print(stale)              # [PosixPath('logs/old/2023.log')]
takeaways: `Path.walk()` (3.12+) yields `(dirpath, dirnames, filenames)` like os.walk
Prune by mutating `dirnames` in place; it skips whole subtrees
`stat().st_size` and `st_mtime` drive size and age based jobs
pitfalls: Using `rglob('*')` and filtering out `.git` afterwards on huge trees; the excluded folders are still fully scanned.

quiz.q: Why is pruning dirnames in Path.walk faster than filtering rglob('*') results?
options: Pruned directories are never listed at all
quiz.explain: Removing a name from dirnames stops walk from descending into that directory.

concepts.name: Pure paths and Windows vs POSIX
concepts.summary: Manipulate paths for another operating system with PurePosixPath and PureWindowsPath, without touching the disk.
concepts.why: Tools that build remote paths (S3 keys, SSH targets, Windows shares from Linux) need the other OS's rules.
concepts.body:
pathlib has two families of classes:

- **Pure paths** (`PurePath`, `PurePosixPath`, `PureWindowsPath`) do only string operations: joining, parts, suffixes, matching. They never touch the file system, so they work for any platform's paths on any platform.
- **Concrete paths** (`Path`, `PosixPath`, `WindowsPath`) add I/O methods. You can only instantiate the concrete class of your own OS; `WindowsPath` on Linux raises `UnsupportedOperation` (3.13).

Use pure paths when the path isn't on the local machine:

- `PurePosixPath("bucket") / "2025" / "a.csv"` for object-store keys or paths on a remote Linux server, even when your code runs on Windows.
- `PureWindowsPath(r"C:\Users\ann\file.txt")` to parse Windows paths received in data on a Linux server.

Windows rules differ: both `\` and `/` are separators, drives and UNC shares form the `anchor` (`C:\`, `\\server\share\`), comparison is case-insensitive, and `p.as_posix()` converts to forward slashes.

`p.as_uri()` turns an absolute path into a `file://` URL, and since 3.13 `Path.from_uri()` parses one back.

Note that pure paths accept any string; they won't tell you a name is invalid on Windows (such as `CON` or one containing `:`).
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath, PureWindowsPath

w = PureWindowsPath(r"C:\Users\Ann\Docs/report.DOCX")
print(w.parts)        # ('C:\\', 'Users', 'Ann', 'Docs', 'report.DOCX')
print(w.drive, w.suffix)               # C: .DOCX
print(w.as_posix())                    # C:/Users/Ann/Docs/report.DOCX
print(w == PureWindowsPath(r"c:\users\ann\docs\REPORT.docx"))  # True

key = PurePosixPath("exports") / "2025" / "sales.csv"   # e.g. an S3 key
print(str(key))                        # exports/2025/sales.csv

uri = Path("/tmp/a b.txt").as_uri()
print(uri)                             # file:///tmp/a%20b.txt
print(Path.from_uri(uri))              # /tmp/a b.txt
takeaways: Pure paths do string-only path logic for any OS; concrete paths add I/O
Use PurePosixPath for remote or object-store paths regardless of the local OS
Windows paths compare case-insensitively and accept both slash styles
pitfalls: Using `Path` (and so local separators) to build S3 keys or remote Linux paths when code may run on Windows.

quiz.q: On Linux, what happens with PureWindowsPath('D:/data') / 'x.txt'?
options: It raises an error because Windows paths are unsupported
quiz.explain: Pure paths are platform-independent string manipulations, usable on any OS.

concepts.name: Matching paths and safe joins
concepts.summary: Test paths against glob patterns with match and full_match, and confine user-supplied paths to a base directory.
concepts.why: Routing files by pattern and preventing path traversal attacks are both matching problems.
concepts.body:
Two ways to test a path against a glob-style pattern without listing directories:

- `p.match(pattern)` matches **from the right** for relative patterns: `Path("a/b/c.py").match("*.py")` and `match("b/*.py")` are both true. `**` is not recursive here; it acts like `*`.
- `p.full_match(pattern)` (3.13) matches the **whole** path and supports recursive `**`: `full_match("src/**/*.py")`. This is the one to use for rules like ignore lists or routing.

Both accept `case_sensitive=`.

Matching is also where path-traversal bugs live. If a web app serves `base / user_input`, then input like `../../etc/passwd` or an absolute path escapes the base. The safe recipe:

1. Join, then `resolve()` to remove `..` and follow symlinks.
2. Check `resolved.is_relative_to(base.resolve())`.
3. Reject otherwise.

Checking the string for `..` is not enough (absolute paths, symlinks, encoded separators). Also reject or normalise empty strings and NUL bytes, which raise `ValueError` in file system calls.

For archives, the same check applies to every member name before extraction; Python 3.12+ `tarfile` offers `filter="data"` (the default from 3.14) for exactly this.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

p = PurePosixPath("src/pkg/util/io.py")
print(p.match("*.py"), p.match("util/*.py"))     # True True
print(p.match("src/*.py"))                       # False
print(p.full_match("src/**/*.py"))               # True
print(p.full_match("*.py"))                      # False

def safe_join(base: Path, user_path: str) -> Path:
    base = base.resolve()
    target = (base / user_path).resolve()
    if not target.is_relative_to(base):
        raise PermissionError(f"outside base: {user_path}")
    return target

Path("public/img").mkdir(parents=True)
print(safe_join(Path("public"), "img/logo.png").name)   # logo.png
for bad in ["../secret.txt", "/etc/passwd", "img/../../x"]:
    try:
        safe_join(Path("public"), bad)
    except PermissionError as e:
        print(e)
takeaways: `match` matches from the right; `full_match` (3.13) matches the whole path with recursive `**`
Resolve then `is_relative_to(base)` to confine user paths
String checks for '..' don't stop path traversal
pitfalls: Serving `base / request_path` without resolving and checking containment.

quiz.q: Which input does a check like `'..' not in user_path` fail to block?
quiz.explain: An absolute path contains no '..' but replaces the base entirely when joined.

concepts.name: Accepting paths in your own APIs
concepts.summary: Design functions that accept str, bytes and PathLike arguments correctly, with accurate type hints.
concepts.why: Library code that only works with one kind of path frustrates users and breaks in surprising ways.
concepts.body:
Callers will pass strings, Path objects, and occasionally other `os.PathLike` objects (from libraries like `py.path` or custom classes). A robust function accepts all of them:

```python
def load(path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> dict:
    path = Path(path)
```

Rules of thumb:

- **Normalise at the boundary**: convert once with `Path(path)` at the top, then work with Path internally.
- If you need a string (for a C library or a subprocess argument), use `os.fspath(path)` rather than `str(path)`. `fspath` accepts only str, bytes and PathLike and raises `TypeError` for other objects, whereas `str()` happily turns `None` or an int into a bogus path.
- Type hints: `str | os.PathLike[str]` is the common annotation; typeshed's `StrPath` alias means the same.
- **Return Path objects** from functions that produce paths; they convert to strings trivially.
- Don't accept bytes paths unless you really need to handle undecodable names; mixing str and bytes in one join raises `TypeError`.

Avoid `isinstance(x, str)` checks to decide whether something is a path: a `str` might be file contents. Make two clearly named parameters or functions instead (`load_file(path)` vs `loads(text)`), the way `json` does.
concepts.code:
import os
from pathlib import Path

def word_count(path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> int:
    path = Path(path)                       # normalise once
    return len(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").split())

class Asset:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    def __fspath__(self): return f"assets/{self.name}"

Path("assets").mkdir()
Path("assets/a.txt").write_text("one two three", encoding="utf-8")
print(word_count("assets/a.txt"))           # 3
print(word_count(Path("assets", "a.txt")))  # 3
print(word_count(Asset("a.txt")))           # 3

print(str(None))                            # None  -- a bogus "path"
try:
    os.fspath(None)
except TypeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)                 # TypeError
takeaways: Accept `str | os.PathLike[str]` and convert with `Path(...)` at the boundary
Use `os.fspath` instead of `str()` when you need a string path
Return Path objects; don't overload one parameter for both paths and contents
pitfalls: Using `str(path)` for conversion, which turns a stray None into a file literally named 'None'.

quiz.q: Why prefer os.fspath(p) over str(p) inside a function that takes a path?
options: It rejects objects that are not paths instead of silently stringifying them
quiz.explain: fspath only accepts str, bytes and os.PathLike, so mistakes surface as TypeError.

concepts.name: Subclassing Path and with_segments
concepts.summary: Extend Path with domain-specific methods using the 3.12+ subclassing support and with_segments.
concepts.why: Custom path types (project roots, virtual file systems, paths carrying context) become clean and type-safe.
concepts.body:
Before 3.12, subclassing `Path` was awkward because it dispatched to `PosixPath`/`WindowsPath` internally. Since 3.12, `Path` and `PurePath` can be subclassed directly, and the subclass is preserved through derived paths: `p / "x"`, `p.parent`, `p.iterdir()` and `p.glob()` all return instances of your class.

They do this through **with_segments(*pathsegments)**, which pathlib calls whenever it constructs a new path from an existing one. The default creates `type(self)(*pathsegments)`. If your subclass carries extra state (pick attribute names that don't clash with existing ones like `root`, `name` or `parts`), such as a project base folder or a session object, accept it in `__init__` and override `with_segments` to pass it along:

```python
def with_segments(self, *segments):
    return type(self)(*segments, base=self.base)
```

Since 3.12, `__init__` receives the path segments and you must call `super().__init__(*args)`; there's no need to override `__new__`.

Good uses: methods like `project_path.is_test_file()`, or a path type for a virtual file system. Keep subclasses thin; behaviour that doesn't depend on the path itself belongs elsewhere.

pathlib's internals changed significantly across 3.12 to 3.14 (`pathlib._abc`, `pathlib.types` in 3.14), so stick to documented hooks rather than private attributes.
takeaways: Since 3.12, Path subclasses survive /, parent, iterdir and glob
Override `with_segments` to carry extra state into derived paths
Call `super().__init__(*args)` and avoid private pathlib internals
pitfalls: Adding state in `__init__` but not overriding `with_segments`, so derived paths lose it and raise TypeError or AttributeError.

quiz.q: In Python 3.12+, what does (MyPath('a') / 'b') return when MyPath subclasses Path?
options: A MyPath instance, created via with_segments
quiz.explain: pathlib builds derived paths through with_segments, which by default uses type(self).

concepts.name: pathlib vs os: performance trade-offs
concepts.summary: Know where pathlib costs more than os and os.path, and how to keep hot file-system loops fast.
concepts.why: Scanning millions of files with naive pathlib code can be several times slower than necessary.
concepts.body:
Path objects are convenient, but each one is a Python object that parses and stores its parts, and many operations create new objects. In typical scripts this cost is irrelevant compared to disk I/O. It starts to matter when you touch hundreds of thousands of paths in a loop.

Where the time goes:

- **Repeated stat calls.** `p.is_file()`, `p.is_dir()` and `p.stat()` each issue a system call. Calling all three per file triples the work. `os.scandir` returns DirEntry objects whose type is usually known from the directory listing itself, with no extra call; `os.walk` and `Path.walk` build on it.
- **Object creation.** `root / name` for every entry allocates a Path and parses it; string joins are cheaper.
- **rglob over huge trees** you'd prune anyway. Prefer `Path.walk` and prune.

Recent releases (3.12 and 3.13) reworked `glob` internally for speed, so upgrading Python can itself help glob-heavy code.

Practical approach: write clear pathlib code first; profile; then, in the hot loop only, drop to `os.scandir` and strings, converting results to Path at the end. Caching `stat` results when you need several fields from the same file also helps.
takeaways: File system calls dominate: avoid redundant stat/is_file calls per entry
`os.scandir` reuses type info from the listing; walk APIs build on it
Write pathlib first, profile, and drop to os/scandir only in hot loops
pitfalls: Calling `exists()`, `is_file()` and `stat()` on the same path in sequence inside a large loop.

quiz.q: Why is os.scandir with entry.is_file() typically faster than Path.iterdir with p.is_file()?
options: DirEntry usually knows the type from the listing, avoiding a stat call per file
Path objects are cached on disk
quiz.explain: The OS reports entry types in the directory listing, and DirEntry keeps that information.
